title: Economic equilibrium

definition.text: A state in which the forces of supply and demand balance, so that prices and quantities stop changing.

facts.text: In a market equilibrium, competition sets a price at which the amount buyers want equals the amount sellers produce.
That price is called the competitive or market-clearing price, and it tends to stay put unless demand or supply changes.
The idea was borrowed from the physical sciences, where balanced forces mean that nothing further changes.
Huw Dixon proposed three properties: agents' behaviour is consistent, no agent wants to change its behaviour, and the equilibrium results from a stable dynamic process.
A price above equilibrium creates a glut that pushes prices down; a price below it creates a shortage that pushes prices up.
When the conditions of demand or supply change, the curves shift and the equilibrium price and quantity change too.
Economists such as Paul Samuelson warn that an equilibrium price is not automatically good: a food market can be in equilibrium while people starve.
During Ireland's Great Famine of 1845–52, food was exported while people starved because the market price was above what Irish farmers could afford.

contested_note: The classical view that free markets always clear on their own has been challenged by economists who point to lasting unemployment and credit rationing.

definition.text: The condition of a market that is not in equilibrium, where the amounts supplied and demanded are out of balance.

facts.text: Disequilibrium can last only a moment or persist for a long time.
Many economists see labour markets as stuck in excess supply over long periods.
Some goods' prices adjust slowly because of menu costs and long-term contracts, but they do not stay out of balance forever.

definition.text: An equilibrium in which several quantities keep growing at the same rate, so that the ratios between them stay fixed.

facts.text: In the neoclassical growth model, output and capital grow at the same rate as the workforce, leaving output per worker unchanged.
Comparing two dynamic equilibria is called comparative dynamics.
In that model a permanently higher saving rate raises capital per worker but leaves the growth rate of output unchanged.

definition.text: The total gain that buyers and sellers get from trading in a market, made up of consumer surplus and producer surplus; also called total or social welfare.

facts.text: The sum of consumer and producer surplus is called social or total surplus, and a fall in that total caused by inefficiency is called deadweight loss.
The engineer Jules Dupuit first put forward the idea in the mid-19th century, and the economist Alfred Marshall made it famous.
It is also called Marshallian surplus, after Alfred Marshall.
On a supply and demand diagram, consumer surplus is the area above the price and below the demand curve, and producer surplus the area below the price and above the supply curve.
Early writers used surplus to study food: farming must feed everyone, so the rest of the economy is limited by the food farmers produce beyond their own needs.

definition.text: The gap between the most a buyer would be willing to pay for something and the price they actually pay.

facts.text: Drinking water usually carries a large consumer surplus: people would pay very high prices for it because they need it to survive.
The first few liters of water are worth the most, since they prevent death, so they hold more surplus than later liters.
Buyers value each extra unit less than the last, yet pay the same market price for every unit, which is where the surplus comes from.
It equals the area under the demand curve and above the price; with a straight-line demand curve it is a triangle, otherwise it is found by integration.
A positive change in consumer surplus after a price change is read as a gain in the person's welfare, a negative change as a loss.
When supply grows and the price falls, existing buyers gain on the units they already bought and new buyers enter and gain too.

definition.text: The gain sellers get when the market price is higher than the least they would accept to supply a good.

facts.text: It is roughly equal to profit, since producers will not normally sell at a loss.
It is shown as the area below the market price line and above the supply curve.
Higher market prices raise it; higher production costs or lower prices shrink it, and taxes, subsidies, new technology and competition can shift it.
It is used to judge how taxes, subsidies, price controls and trade policies affect producers.

definition.text: A shortcut that estimates the change in consumer surplus from a small change in supply when the demand curve stays the same.

facts.text: With straight-line demand, the change in surplus is a trapezoid whose height is the price change and whose middle width is the average of the quantities before and after.
